title: Seva with neighbors
hook: serving alongside people of every faith
tomorrow: creek, food bank, tutoring: Simran can't keep all three. which one?

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva for the earth: air the Guru, water the father, the earth the great mother. Simran pulled the cart out. Then a van pulled in.
screen: `SEVA FOR THE EARTH.` → `THEN A VAN PULLED IN.`

segments.voice: Simran stays. The van belongs to a church youth group in matching orange shirts, and Maya's cousin climbs out of it. By noon a family from the mosque across town shows up with a cooler of water. So Simran is sorting cans beside a boy wearing a cross, and she remembers something odd in her own gutka. Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib there are shaloks signed with a name that isn't a Guru's: Farid, a Muslim Sufi. In the Sikh scripture. Why is he there?
screen: `AN ORANGE-SHIRT CHURCH CREW.` → `WATER FROM THE MOSQUE.` → `WHY IS FARID IN THE GRANTH?`

segments.voice: Farid isn't alone. The Guru Granth Sahib holds the words of the Gurus and also of bhagats, saints from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, among them Kabir, Ravidas, Namdev and Farid. Guru Arjan, who compiled it, set their hymns inside the Sikh scripture itself. Here's one way to solve the puzzle, from Guru Arjan's own words on Ang 1299, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I get along with everyone. And in Akal Ustat, a composition tradition credits to Guru Gobind Singh, there's a line Sikhs hold close: manas ki jaat sabhai ekai pahichanbo. Recognize the whole human race as one. So the book on the gurdwara's throne is already a shared table. But it's not a blur. Farid's verses keep his name, and in places a Guru's shalok answers his, side by side, with the Gurus' teaching as the frame. That's seva with neighbors too. Simran doesn't stop being a Sikh to carry a bag next to a Christian kid or a Muslim family. She brings her reasons, they bring theirs, and the creek gets clean. One to tell a friend tonight: the Sikh scripture has a Muslim saint's verses inside it.
screen: `BHAGATS: SAINTS INSIDE THE GRANTH.` · `NO ENEMY, NO STRANGER.` · `ONE HUMAN RACE.` · `SIDE BY SIDE, NOT A BLUR.` · then, large: `SERVE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Run a small plan in your head during the sit. First the wish: one project near you where neighbors of other faiths already serve, a food pantry, a park day, a blood drive. Then the one thing most likely to stop you joining. Then the plan: when that obstacle shows up, what you'll do instead.
Seva with neighbors. Serving beside people of every faith, keeping your own reasons, because no one is a stranger.
Keep this one: serve together, with your reasons and theirs, and one creek between you. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1710 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 84 OF 134.` → `TOMORROW: SIMRAN CAN'T KEEP ALL THREE. WHICH ONE?`

howItsDone: Sikh groups join interfaith service days, food drives and relief work alongside churches, mosques, temples and synagogues, and the gurdwara langar is open to anyone who comes.

chat.meaning: Guru Arjan wrote that no one is an enemy or a stranger, and Akal Ustat says recognize one human race. Serving together fits.

gutka.meaning: a small book of daily Sikh prayers

bhagats.meaning: saints whose hymns are included in the Guru Granth Sahib

Farid.meaning: a Muslim Sufi saint whose shaloks are in the Granth

Akal Ustat.meaning: 'praise of the Timeless One', a composition credited to Guru Gobind Singh

Kabir.meaning: a bhagat whose hymns appear in the Guru Granth Sahib

Unity thread (owner, 2026-10-14, 'one human race'): this lesson carries 'manas ki jaat sabhai ekai pahichanbo'. Akal Ustat is in the Dasam Granth; its attribution to Guru Gobind Singh is accepted by many Sikhs and questioned by some, hence 'a composition tradition credits to Guru Gobind Singh'. Confirm the transliteration and the line's place (often cited as Akal Ustat 85).
Confirm Ang 1299 (Kanara, Guru Arjan) for 'naa ko bairee nahee bigaanaa' and the paraphrase.
Confirm that Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth with bhagat bani, and that among Farid's shaloks some are answered by shaloks of Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das or Guru Arjan.
